**The Keeper of Gannet Rock**

For thirty-one years, Elias Marrow climbed the one hundred and fourteen iron steps of Gannet Rock Light twice a day. He climbed them at dusk to light the lamp and at dawn to put it out. He knew each step by its sound. The fortieth rang a little higher than the others, and the ninety-second had a hairline crack that whined in cold weather.

The lighthouse sat on a black knuckle of basalt four miles off the Cornish coast. A supply boat came every second Thursday, weather permitting, which in winter meant hardly ever. Elias didn't mind. He had his logbook, his tins of paraffin, a shelf of water-stained novels, and the sea. The sea changed so often that he never found it boring.

His wife, Maren, had lived there with him for the first nineteen years. She kept a garden in wooden crates sheltered behind the oil store: potatoes, stubborn kale, and one rosebush that bloomed every June no matter how hard the salt wind blew. When she died, the supply boat carried her back to the mainland. Elias stayed. He told the Trinity House inspector it was because nobody else knew the lamp's temperament. The truth was that he couldn't picture where else he would go.

He kept watering the rose.

In the autumn of his thirty-first year, a letter arrived with the supply boat. The light was being automated. Engineers would come in spring to install an electric beacon, solar panels, and a radio link to a control room in Harwich. Elias would be pensioned off with gratitude and a small brass plaque.

He read the letter three times, folded it, and used it as a bookmark.

The storm came on the ninth of November. It built all afternoon, with the barometer falling faster than Elias had ever seen, and by nightfall the waves were throwing spray over the gallery rail, sixty feet above the rocks. He lit the lamp at 4:47 p.m. and stayed in the lantern room, trimming the wick and wiping salt from the inside of the glass as the tower hummed around him.

At a quarter past midnight, the radio crackled. A fishing trawler, the *Kittiwake*, had lost her engine and was drifting toward the Mawls, a shelf of reef south of the Rock. Her skipper sounded young and very frightened. Their GPS had failed when the wheelhouse flooded, and all they could see was the light.

Elias took the handset. "Keep my light off your port bow," he said, "and count the flashes. Three every fifteen seconds. If it ever turns into a steady beam, you're too close to the reef. Turn hard away."

The old lens worked just that way. At a certain angle, the red sector glass turned the flashing light into a steady warning beam. Maren used to call it the lighthouse's frown.

For two hours he talked the boy through it, in a slow and steady voice, the way Maren used to talk to him through the long winters. When the flashes turned steady, Elias told him to steer hard to starboard. The *Kittiwake* dropped anchor in the lee of Pendower Head just before three. Her crew was cold and bruised, and all of them were alive.

In the spring, the engineers came as promised. They were polite and efficient, and they looked at the brass lamp the way people look at a rotary telephone.

On his last morning, Elias climbed the steps one final time and listened for the fortieth to ring. Then he went down to the garden behind the oil store and dug up the rosebush, roots and soil and all, and wrapped it in sackcloth.

The supply boat was waiting. The skipper of the *Kittiwake* was on board. He had asked to crew that run, and he reached out a hand to help the old keeper aboard.

Behind them, the new light blinked on in the daylight, ready for the dark.
